title: Gas Lamps in Berlin - FAQ
subtitle: How many are left, which ones stay, and why the city is switching them off.

items.q: How many gas lamps are left in Berlin?
items.a: The city's public lighting register lists **16,332 gas lamps** (checked on 10 November 2026), of which **15,728 are burning**. In July 2025 the Senate reported 17,400. Before the conversion began there were about **44,000**.

items.q: Will all of Berlin's gas lamps be converted to LED?
items.a: Most of them. Only about **3,300** in protected areas agreed in 2013 are meant to stay on gas. The Senate says there is **no end date** for converting the rest, and in 2025 it asked the heritage office to review the protected areas as well.

items.q: Why does Berlin still have so many gas lamps?
items.a: Largely because of **West Berlin**. While the East moved to sodium-vapour lamps, thousands of western side streets kept gas. About **95 per cent** of today's gas lamps stand in the former West.

items.q: Why is Berlin replacing its gas lamps?
items.a: Cost and energy. A four-flame gas lamp used about **470 euro** of energy in 2024, the LED replacement about **25 euro**. Converting one lamp costs about **10,000 euro** and pays back in roughly **12 years**, according to the Senate.

items.q: Can you see East and West Berlin from space?
items.a: Yes, in the street lights. A photo from the **International Space Station on 6 April 2013** shows orange sodium light in most of the East and whiter light in the West. LED conversion is slowly erasing the difference.

items.q: Where can I see gas lamps in Berlin?
items.a: The **Chamissoplatz** quarter in Kreuzberg, the centre of **Charlottenburg** around Sophie-Charlotten-Straße, Alt-Tegel, the old town of **Spandau** and Onkel Toms Hütte all sit inside protected areas. The map in this post shows every street.
